verification.note: Unit 1 (Solid State) is sourced from the chemistry half of "FAST TRACK IPE for Sr. Students", book pp.62-64, which prints the question and a model answer. The 1+1 mark split is a CLAIM, not the board's, until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. Neither the two-book union check nor a board back-test was possible for Chemistry-II: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is physics-only and first-year, and no second-year chemistry paper is in the corpus. The book prints the question as "Define the term amorphous ?"; the stray space and question mark on an imperative are normalised here. The book gives only the definition and three examples; the two extra properties in step 2 (isotropic, no sharp melting point) are added from NCERT because they are the usual second marking point.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The definition
lines: An amorphous solid is one in which the
constituent particles are arranged in an
It has short range order only, and no long
The word comes from Greek and means
steps.why: The whole idea of an amorphous solid is the ABSENCE of long range order. The particles are ordered over a few atomic distances (short range order) and then the pattern is lost, so the definition has to say both parts: irregular arrangement, short range order only.
common_mistakes: Writing that the particles are arranged in no order at all. There is short range order; it is the long range order that is missing.
Calling an amorphous solid a true liquid. It is called a pseudo solid, or a super cooled liquid, because it does flow very slowly, but it is still a solid with a definite shape and volume.
steps.memory_tip: a- means without, morph means form. Amorphous = without a regular form.
steps.margin_note: Say "irregular arrangement" and "short range order". Both phrases are needed for the definition mark.

steps.label: Examples and properties
lines: They are isotropic: physical properties are
They soften over a range of temperature
instead of melting at one sharp point.
steps.why: An example is a separate marking point in a two-mark question, and the two properties follow directly from the irregular arrangement: with no ordered direction the properties cannot depend on direction, and with bonds of many different strengths the solid softens gradually rather than melting at one temperature.
common_mistakes: Giving quartz or common salt as the example. Both are crystalline solids, so they are the opposite case.
Writing that amorphous solids have a sharp melting point. That belongs to crystalline solids.
steps.memory_tip: Glass is the standard example. Window glass softens slowly when heated, it does not melt at one temperature.
steps.margin_note: One named example is enough for the mark. The isotropic and softening points are the extra content that lifts a bare answer.

insider_note: Two marks means two separate points, so never stop at the definition. Write the irregular arrangement with short range order, then a named example such as glass.
